Gergely Szegedi
ger'ge-ly se'ge-dee
n. (Gergely Szegedi, c. 1511–1569, Hungarian Reformed preacher at Debrecen and Nagyvarad, and a writer against the antitrinitarians)
Szegedi, Hungarian, of Szeged, the town on the Tisza; Gergely, the Hungarian form of Gregory, from Greek gregoreo, to watch, to be vigilant.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Gergely Szegedi was a Franciscan of Hungarian birth who was drawn to the Reformation, studied at Wittenberg, and served as preacher at Gyula, Debrecen and Nagyvarad in the years when the Hungarian church was passing from the Lutheran to the Reformed confession under the Turkish and Transylvanian partition of the kingdom. He is remembered for the second of his two fights. The first was with Rome, carried on from the pulpit; the second was with the antitrinitarians, who after 1565 made headway in Transylvania and the Partium under the protection of the prince's physician and the preaching of Ferenc David, and who had to be answered in Hungarian by men the common people would read. Szegedi wrote that answer, setting the eternal deity of the Son and the Spirit from the plain places of Scripture rather than from the schoolmen, and he stood with Peter Melius and the Debrecen party at the disputations where the two confessions parted for good. He died in 1569, the year before the great debate at Nagyvarad. His name belongs in the dictionary because the Hungarian Reformation's hardest hour was not its struggle with the Mass but its struggle for the Trinity, and the men who held that line in a language with almost no theological vocabulary of its own were doing original work.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines the Trinity as the union of three persons in one Godhead; a heretic as one who holds an opinion repugnant to the established faith; and to confute as to disprove, to overthrow by argument.

expand to see more

TRINITY, n. [L. trinitas.] The union of three persons in one Godhead, or the three persons of the Father, Son and Holy Ghost in one divine nature.

HERETIC, n. [Gr. to choose.] A person under any religion, but particularly the Christian, who holds and teaches opinions repugnant to the established faith.

CONFUTE, v.t. [L. confuto.] To disprove; to prove to be false or defective; to overthrow by argument or evidence.

PREACHER, n. One who discourses publicly on religious subjects; one who inculcates any thing with earnestness.

GODHEAD, n. Godship; deity; divinity; divine nature or essence; applied to the true God.

Key Scripture

Joh 1:1 — "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."

Col 2:9 — "For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily."

1Jo 2:22 — "Who is a liar but he that denieth that Jesus is the Christ? He is antichrist, that denieth the Father and the Son."

Tit 1:9 — "Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers."

Modern Corruption

Debrecen and Nagyvarad preacher who wrote against the Transylvanian antitrinitarians in Hungarian, for readers who had no Latin.

expand to see more

The corruption named here is antitrinitarianism as it took hold in Transylvania after 1565: the denial that the Son and the Spirit are God in the same sense as the Father, taught by Ferenc David and organised by Giorgio Biandrata, and granted standing by the Diet of Torda. It is not a nuance within Christianity. “Who is a liar but he that denieth that Jesus is the Christ? He is antichrist, that denieth the Father and the Son” (1Jo 2:22) is the apostle's own classification, and the dictionary keeps it. The modern descendants of this error—Unitarianism, and the liberal theology which keeps the word God and empties the word Son—stand under the same judgment.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of Szegedi himself. The principle to recover is that the Trinity is defended in the vernacular or it is not defended at all. Szegedi wrote in Hungarian because the men being misled read Hungarian. A church whose doctrine of God lives only in its ministers' Latin has already lost the argument in its own pews.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek logos (G3056), the Word; Greek theotes (G2320), deity, the state of being God.

expand to see more

Greek logos (G3056) — word, discourse, reason; “In the beginning was the Word”, John 1:1.

Greek theos (G2316) — God; “and the Word was God”, John 1:1.

Greek theotes (G2320) — deity, godhead, the essence of God; “all the fulness of the Godhead bodily”, Colossians 2:9.

Greek antichristos (G500) — against Christ, in the place of Christ; “He is antichrist, that denieth the Father and the Son”, 1 John 2:22.

Greek antilego (G483) — to speak against, to gainsay; “to convince the gainsayers”, Titus 1:9.

Usage

"“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (Joh 1:1) — the line held in Hungarian against the Transylvanian antitrinitarians."

"“He is antichrist, that denieth the Father and the Son” (1Jo 2:22) — the apostle's own classification of the error."

"“to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9) — preacher at Gyula, Debrecen and Nagyvarad."
